sources.what: Kingsbury Ordnance Plant (FUDS IN59799F357000): 6 hazardous sites, highest risk 'High'; active site 03HTRW: groundwater (High) with TNT 0.71 ug/L, RDX 39.0, mercury 230.0, arsenic 3400.0, lead 78500.0 ug/L; soil (Medium) arsenic 11.1, lead 14.8 mg/kg; active site 04OEW (unexploded munitions and ordnance area): soil (High) TNT 0.53, RDX 4.17, HMX 2480, arsenic 163.0, mercury 167.0, lead 2000.0 mg/kg; groundwater (Medium) arsenic 26.2, RDX 39.0 ug/L; final cleanup action Sep. 2040, monitoring until Sep. 2072; land: about 7,100 acres in the Kingsbury Fish and Wildlife Area, about 5,000 commercial/industrial; Fisher-Calo Superfund site on part of the former DoD-owned Kingsbury Industrial Development Park. sourcing_note: New short, Nov. 16, 2026, Scoop: 'remake kingsbury and kingsford heights to include how toxic and contaminated from the munitions plant it is'. The Nov. 7/15 Kingsbury short (kingsbury-ordnance-plant) already aired; this one tells what the plant left behind. Plant history lines reuse the checked Nov. 7 short's facts: 1940, the Army picked the land; more than 13,000 acres of farms; loaded shells for World War 2; a second run for Korea, then shut down for good (WKVI; Indiana Public Media; The History Museum; Towne Post; La Porte Herald-Dispatch). Line 1, 'Defense Department cleanup data listed them in the ground here': ProPublica's Bombs in Your Backyard page for the plant (FUDS IN59799F357000) is built from fiscal 2015 Defense Environmental Restoration Program data: lead, arsenic, mercury and the explosives TNT, RDX and HMX in soil and groundwater at both active sites (see the Kingsford Heights storyboard for the numbers); past tense and the credit's '2015' because that is the data's year; the EPA says soil and groundwater contamination was found at the old plant's industrial park; the DNR marks contaminated areas. Line 4, Fisher-Calo: a solvent reclaiming company on the old plant grounds (the Kingsbury Industrial Development Park) from late 1972 (EPA NPL narrative) / 'the early 1970s' (EPA reuse page); 'Wastes were buried on-site in over 10,000 drums' (NPL narrative, conditions at listing, Dec. 1982); the cleanup excavated buried drums (EPA reuse page; EPA's 2025 five-year review notice). Counts differ between EPA records, so 'thousands', and all the drum facts are EPA's, so 'the EPA says'. 'Starting in the 1970s' because the burial isn't dated more closely than 1972 to 1982. NPL final Sept. 1983. Line 5: the EPA's 2022 Explanation of Significant Differences 'documented the need for institutional controls to prevent exposure to contaminated groundwater' (EPA reuse page): one EPA record, attributed. Line 7: the Defense Department's FY2025 Defense Environmental Restoration Program table (Table 7, posted June 2026) lists the plant: IRP, 4 sites, final response complete FY2009, $0 to complete; MMRP (military munitions), 1 site, final response complete FY2046, $193K to complete. One record, so 'the Defense Department's latest report projects'. Left out: the old 2040/2072 dates (ProPublica's FY2015 data, superseded); 'still in the soil and groundwater' (the blind check said it overstated what current records show); drinking-water wells (one record's note, possibly dated); health effects (no source ties illness to the site). Pictures: the dark patch sinks straight down and stays put, with nothing built over it; the drums are drawn half-buried, as in the 1970s, not the later dig; the bunkers are generic earth-covered igloos (Indiana Landmarks: 'parallel rows of abandoned ammunition bunkers'); the DNR's real sign wording isn't known, so no sign is drawn and the map legend's words are on a quote card. Blind check Nov. 16 (first version) and its fixes: 'still' cut; 2040/2072 replaced by the FY2025 table's 2046; 'more than 10,000' became 'thousands'; credits dated 2015. Second blind check Nov. 16 (script, text and pictures only): lines 1-6 supported (line 1 rests on ProPublica's 2015 DoD data alone, so past tense and the 2015 credit stay; line 5 could be read in only one EPA record, so it stays attributed to the EPA). Line 7 was 'the Defense Department's latest report projects its munitions cleanup here will last until 2046': no FY2025 Annual Report to Congress is posted yet (the FY2025 status tables are), and Indiana's open FUDS munitions site is still in investigation, not cleanup, so it now says 'latest data says its munitions work here won't end until 2046' (the FY2024 table said 2036 and ProPublica's 2015 data 2040, so commenters may quote those). The groundwater picture now shows the patch spreading sideways toward the well (ATSDR: three plumes under Fisher-Calo moving south-southwest); the EPA's 2000 five-year review says about 3,500 buried drums were dug up and removed in 1995, which the post text says. The 2046 picture is now the old plant grounds at dusk (bunkers could suggest stored munitions). Credits: the Herald-Dispatch (no article found) and Towne Post (repeats the History Museum) dropped; DoD credit names the FY2025 status tables (Table 7). Third check (of the changes), Nov. 16: line 7 'munitions work here won't end' could be heard as making munitions and 2046 is a projection, so it now says 'latest data projects its munitions cleanup here won't be finished until 2046', typed '2046 (PROJECTED)'; 'here' cut from line 2 for length. Everything else, credits and pictures fine.

beats.text: Lead. Arsenic. Mercury. Explosives. Defense Department cleanup data listed them in the ground here. This was the Kingsbury Ordnance Plant.
beats.label: LAPORTE COUNTY, INDIANA
beats.credit: ProPublica (Defense Department cleanup data, 2015); Indiana DNR

beats.text: In 1940, the Army picked more than 13,000 acres of farmland for a plant that would load shells for World War 2.
beats.label: KINGSBURY ORDNANCE PLANT
beats.credit: WKVI; Indiana Public Media; The History Museum, South Bend

beats.text: It ran again for Korea, then shut down for good.
beats.label: AFTER THE WAR
beats.credit: WKVI; The History Museum, South Bend

beats.text: Starting in the 1970s, a solvent company on the old grounds buried thousands of drums of waste, the EPA says. It became a Superfund site.
beats.label: FISHER-CALO SUPERFUND SITE
beats.credit: U.S. EPA (NPL site narrative; Superfund Sites in Reuse)

beats.text: In 2022, the EPA called for controls to prevent exposure to its contaminated groundwater.
beats.label: KINGSBURY INDUSTRIAL PARK
beats.credit: U.S. EPA, Superfund Sites in Reuse in Indiana (2022 decision)

beats.text: Part of the old plant is a state wildlife area now. Its map marks some spots: Contaminated Area. No Trespassing.
beats.label: KINGSBURY FISH & WILDLIFE AREA
beats.credit: Indiana DNR, Kingsbury Fish & Wildlife Area maps (2022, 2025)

beats.text: And the Defense Department's latest data projects its munitions cleanup here won't be finished until 2046.
beats.label: THE OLD PLANT GROUNDS
beats.credit: Defense Department, FY2025 cleanup status tables (Table 7)
